title: Weaker Protective Association Between Higher Income and Medical Bill Payment Difficulties and Related Inability to Afford Basic Necessities Among Black than White Adults in California
content: Higher income may be associated with lower medical financial hardship, but this association may differ by race. Guided by Minorities’ Diminished Returns (MDRs), we examined two related outcomes among Black and White adults in California: medical bill payment difficulties and inability to afford basic necessities due to medical bills among adults reporting payment difficulties. We used annual California Health Interview Survey estimates for 2017–2024, comparing income below versus at or above 400% of the federal poverty level. We calculated relative reductions first and absolute contrasts second, using equally weighted annual mean prevalences. For payment difficulties, relative reductions were smaller among Black than White adults in 2017–2024 (47.7% versus 58.0%) and 2019–2024 (45.6% versus 58.3%). Full-period absolute reductions were also smaller (6.96 versus 8.29 percentage points). For inability to afford necessities, the 2019–2024 relative reduction was smaller among Black adults (38.2% versus 43.4%), while absolute reductions were similar (16.0 versus 15.6 points). The smaller relative reduction among Black adults was consistent with MDRs. The two outcomes have different denominators. Future research should formally test race-by-income interactions when respondent-level survey data and design information become available; these tests were not possible using the supplied online-analysis exports.
